candidates.title: Verifier-Augmented LLM for Multi-Vendor CLI Generation
candidates.research_question: Does integrating a deterministic network verifier into an iterative generate–verify–repair loop with an LLM reduce semantic and topological configuration errors across multi-vendor CLI tasks compared with LLM-only generation?
hypotheses: An LLM paired with a deterministic verifier and a single verification-feedback repair loop will produce network configurations with fewer semantic errors than the same LLM without verifier assistance.
Verifier-augmented generation will reduce topological misconfigurations (e.g., unintended reachability changes) by a clinically meaningful margin compared with LLM-only outputs.
candidates.proposed_design: Preregistered controlled experiment using a synthetic multi-vendor configuration task set (Cisco IOS-like and Juniper-like CLIs) drawn from public NetOps benchmarks and generated scenarios (n=120 tasks). Two arms: (A) LLM-only generation with a fixed prompt; (B) LLM + deterministic verifier (Batfish or equivalent) in a single generate–verify–repair loop where verifier outputs are converted to localized repair prompts and the LLM is allowed one repair iteration. Use a hosted LLM API (single model family) with fixed temperature and seed policy. All configurations are validated offline in simulator/emulator; no live devices are modified. Metrics: verifier pass/fail (reachability, policy compliance), syntactic success, repair iterations required, and error taxonomy. Preregister seeds, retry policy (max 1 retry for transient API failure), and stopping rules. Record all prompts, model outputs, verifier traces, and hashes.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task verifier pass binary labels, counts of semantic/topological errors, syntactic error counts, number of repair iterations, and per-task latency/model-call counts. Aggregate pass rates per arm with per-task error annotations and representative failing examples.
candidates.primary_outcome: Difference in verifier pass rate (proportion of tasks passing all deterministic checks) between LLM+verifier loop and LLM-only, assessed at task level.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute proportions and 95% confidence intervals for pass rates in each arm. Use two-sided chi-squared or Fisher exact test for pass-rate comparison. Estimate absolute risk reduction and number-needed-to-repair. Report effect sizes (Cohen's h) and bootstrap CIs for nonparametric metrics. Perform error-type stratified analysis (syntactic vs semantic vs topological) and qualitative failure-mode taxonomy with representative examples. Report per-task model-call cost and latency.
risks: Deterministic verifier coverage may not fully capture control-plane dynamics, causing false negatives or positives in the offline simulator.
Vendor-CLI heterogeneity could cause translation errors unrelated to LLM reasoning, confounding attribution.
Exposure of representative failing prompts and repair patterns could assist adversarial actors if shared without limits.

candidates.title: Adversarial Prompt Stress Test for Generate–Verify NetOps Pipelines
candidates.research_question: How susceptible are LLM-driven generate–verify NetOps pipelines to adversarial and prompt-injection attacks, and which mitigation (input sanitization, strict prompt templates, verifier hardening) most reduces successful unsafe outputs?
hypotheses: Adversarially crafted prompts will increase the rate of unsafe or policy-violating configuration outputs even when a deterministic verifier is present in the pipeline.
Combining input sanitization with stricter verifier checks will reduce but not eliminate successful adversarial cases compared with an unmitigated pipeline.
candidates.proposed_design: Construct an adversarial prompt corpus (n=150 adversarial variants) derived from documented prompt-injection patterns and non-adversarial controls (n=150) following prior attack taxonomies. Evaluate three pipeline conditions on the same task set: (1) baseline LLM + verifier, (2) LLM + input sanitization + verifier, (3) LLM + verifier with hardened acceptance criteria (e.g., semantic invariants). Run each adversarial and control prompt once per condition; all execution in simulator. Metrics: fraction of prompts producing verifier-accepted but unsafe configurations (unsafe=violates security policy or introduces unintended reachability), verifier false-negative rate, and types of attack success. Preregister adversarial generation rules, sanitizer rules, verifier acceptance thresholds, seeds, and retry policies.
candidates.expected_data: Per-prompt condition labels indicating attack success, verifier decisions, sanitized prompt versions, resulting configurations, and annotated failure modes. Summary counts of false negatives and mitigation effectiveness percentages per condition.
candidates.primary_outcome: Proportion of adversarial prompts that yield verifier-accepted but unsafe configurations (i.e., false negatives) under each mitigation condition; statistical comparison of mitigation effectiveness.
candidates.analysis_outline: Paired analysis comparing false-negative proportions across conditions using McNemar's test and compute relative risk reduction with 95% CIs. Analyze distribution of attack vectors that bypass each mitigation. Report verifier error types and compute attacker success rate per attack class. Conduct sensitivity analysis varying verifier strictness and sanitizer aggressiveness.
risks: Creation and sharing of adversarial prompts could be dual-use and enable attacks if distributed without safeguards.
Simulator-based evaluation may underestimate attack success or overestimate mitigation effectiveness in production.
Mitigations (e.g., heavy sanitization) might degrade legitimate operator inputs, causing availability or usability issues.

candidates.title: Prompt-Uncertainty Ensembles to Predict Verification Failure in NetOps
candidates.research_question: Can ensemble generation with uncertainty metrics (prompt-ensemble disagreement and model-calibrated scores) reliably predict verifier failure for LLM-produced NetOps configurations, enabling an automated escalation threshold?
hypotheses: An ensemble of diversified prompts will produce a measurable disagreement score that correlates with verification failure probability.

A calibrated classifier combining ensemble disagreement and model-provided confidence scores can achieve operationally useful discrimination (AUC substantially above 0.7) for predicting verifier failures.
candidates.proposed_design: Generate a dataset of NetOps tasks (n=200) covering varied difficulty. For each task, produce k=5 outputs using a prompt family (controlled paraphrases and schema vs freeform) to create an ensemble. Compute disagreement metrics (syntactic diff, semantic reachability differences) and derive model-native scores (logprob aggregates). Label outputs with deterministic verifier pass/fail. Train a small logistic regression on 70% data to predict verifier fail using ensemble features; evaluate on 30% holdout. Predefine calibration targets (e.g., threshold ensuring false-negative rate <5%) and decision rules. Record all artifacts and seeds.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task ensemble outputs, computed disagreement and confidence metrics, verifier labels, trained classifier coefficients, ROC curve, AUC, Brier score, and selected threshold with confusion matrix on holdout.
candidates.primary_outcome: Classifier discrimination performance (AUC) and calibration at the predefined escalation threshold; demonstrate a threshold achieving target false-negative rate if feasible.
candidates.analysis_outline: Report AUC with 95% CI via bootstrapping, Brier score for calibration, calibration plots, and decision-curve analysis to quantify net benefit at candidate thresholds. Perform ablation to measure contribution of disagreement vs model confidence. Report operational trade-offs (false positives leading to unnecessary escalation).
risks: Prompt-ensemble construction choices may inadvertently encode task-specific biases leading to overoptimistic performance.
Calibration measured in simulation may not generalize to production models or different prompt families.
Ensemble and classifier overhead increases model-call cost and latency, affecting operational feasibility.

candidates.title: Minimal Verification Contract for Limited Autonomous NetOps Actions
candidates.research_question: What minimal set of deterministic acceptance checks (a verification contract) is sufficient to safely allow limited autonomous LLM-driven changes for low-risk NetOps tasks under simulator evaluation?
hypotheses: A compact verification contract consisting of syntax checking, reachability-preservation, and automated rollback verification will produce a low rate of unsafe outcomes for a defined low-risk task class.
Adding rollback verification yields diminishing returns beyond reachability-preservation for the selected low-risk tasks.
candidates.proposed_design: Define a low-risk task class (non-routing VLAN adjustments, isolated ACL changes to test VLANs, and benign interface descriptions) and a set of candidate verification contracts of increasing strictness: (C0) syntax only, (C1) syntax + reachability invariants, (C2) C1 + rollback simulation. Generate n=100 tasks from public datasets and simulated operational scenarios. For each task, allow LLM to propose a change and apply the contract checks in simulator; if contract passes, simulate rollback and verify no state corruption. Compare the proportion of tasks passing contract and subsequently verified to be safe under each contract. Predefine operator-acceptance proxy (e.g., acceptable unsafe rate <2%).
candidates.expected_data: Per-task contract pass/fail, simulation rollback success/failure, counts of unsafe events post-acceptance, and marginal improvement when adding checks. Cost (model calls, verifier time) per contract.
candidates.primary_outcome: Proportion of accepted changes that are both verifier-compliant and rollback-successful under each contract; assessment whether minimal contract meets operator-acceptance proxy.
candidates.analysis_outline: Estimate proportions with 95% CIs and compare contracts using paired proportion tests (McNemar or exact methods). Compute marginal utility and cost per added check. Present sensitivity analysis varying the operator-acceptance proxy (1%–5%). Provide representative failure cases and discuss whether contract generalizes beyond low-risk tasks.
risks: Operator-acceptance proxy is a surrogate and may not reflect real human risk tolerance; conclusions may not transfer to production.
Simulator rollback success may not capture complex stateful control-plane behaviors present in live networks.
Narrow task class may overstate contract effectiveness when confronted with broader operational tasks.
